entities.name: Thoreau
entities.body: The book's narrator, recounting the two years he spent living alone in a self-built cabin at Walden Pond. Written entirely in the first person, the book never names him; per editorial policy, a memoir's own narrator is not cast as a spoken-of character, so this entry carries no bindable alias.

entities.name: John Field
entities.body: An honest, hard-working, but shiftless Irish tenant farmer at the Baker Farm, visited during a thunderstorm in Chapter 10; Thoreau tries, without success, to persuade him that his laborious pursuit of tea, coffee, and meat is what keeps him poor.

entities.name: Cato
entities.body: Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder, the Roman statesman and agricultural writer, quoted four times on farming and household management from his De Re Rustica -- including the recipe Thoreau follows for his own kneaded bread. Never confused in the text with Cato Ingraham, the formerly enslaved Concord resident of Chapter 14, who is bound separately and carries no global alias.

entities.name: Cato Ingraham
entities.body: A formerly enslaved man, held by Duncan Ingraham of Concord village, who built him a house and let him live in Walden Woods; Thoreau notes the half-obliterated cellar hole that was his home, and that he is not to be confused with either Roman Cato -- "Cato, not Uticensis, but Concordiensis."

entities.name: Brister Freeman
entities.body: A formerly enslaved man, "a handy Negro," held by Squire Cummings, who planted the apple trees still bearing wild fruit on Brister's Hill; his gravestone in the old Lincoln burying-ground styles him "Sippio Brister" -- a name Thoreau hears echoing Scipio Africanus.

entities.name: Fenda
entities.body: Brister Freeman's wife, "large, round, and black," who told fortunes hospitably and shared his house on Brister's Hill.

entities.name: Zilpha
entities.body: A colored woman who spun linen for the townsfolk in a small house near Thoreau's bean-field, singing shrilly as she worked; her dwelling was burned by English prisoners of war in 1812 while she was away, killing her cat, dog, and hens.

entities.name: Hugh Quoil
entities.body: The last inhabitant of Walden Woods before Thoreau, an Irish ditcher known as "Col. Quoil," reputed to have fought at Waterloo; a man of manners and civil speech despite his poverty and trembling delirium, he died in the road at the foot of Brister's Hill shortly after Thoreau's arrival.

entities.name: John Farmer
entities.body: A parable figure of Chapter 11: a laborer who, resting after a hard day's work, hears a flute and feels called to a higher life than his "mean moiling" one, though he cannot see how to answer the call beyond a new austerity of mind.

entities.name: Hermit
entities.body: Thoreau's own voice in Chapter 12's staged dialogue -- a would-be contemplative interrupted mid-meditation by the Poet's proposal to go fishing, and unable to resist.

entities.name: Poet
entities.body: The Hermit's fishing companion in Chapter 12's staged dialogue, identified with no other name; real-world scholarship reads him as Thoreau's friend and fellow writer William Ellery Channing, but the text itself never supplies that name.

entities.name: Duncan Ingraham
entities.body: A gentleman of Concord village who enslaved Cato Ingraham and built him the house in Walden Woods where he was permitted to live.

entities.name: Squire Cummings
entities.body: The Concord man who enslaved Brister Freeman.

entities.name: the Stratton family
entities.body: A former-inhabitant family whose homestead and orchard once covered the slope of Brister's Hill, named only by surname, with no individual member identified; not to be confused with Hezekiah Stratton, named later in the ledger excerpt of Chapter 15.

entities.name: the Breed family
entities.body: A former-inhabitant family whose hut, the site of a famous local house-fire Thoreau describes at length, stood near the edge of the wood closer to the village.

entities.name: Nutting and Le Grosse
entities.body: Two former inhabitants named together, who lived where a well and lilac bushes still mark an open field; nothing else is told of them. Not to be confused with Sam Nutting, named later in Chapter 15.

entities.name: Wyman the potter
entities.body: A potter who squatted farther into the woods than any other former inhabitant, furnished the town with earthenware, and left descendants who continued the trade after him; the last inhabitant before Hugh Quoil, who occupied "Wyman's tenement."

entities.name: Wyman the younger
entities.body: Wyman the potter's descendant, who continued the family trade and later disappeared; a travelling pottery-dealer who had once bought a wheel from him stops to ask Thoreau what became of him.

entities.name: Sam Nutting
entities.body: A bear-hunter on Fair Haven Ledges who traded skins for rum in Concord village and once claimed to have seen a moose there; owner of the famous fox-hound Burgoyne. Not to be confused with the unrelated former-inhabitant family of the same surname in Chapter 14.

entities.name: Burgoyne
entities.body: Sam Nutting's famous fox-hound, borrowed by Thoreau's informant; Nutting himself pronounced the name "Bugine."

entities.name: Hezekiah Stratton
entities.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a wild-cat skin in 1743; a sergeant in the French war, and so not one who would have gotten credit for hunting less noble game. Not to be confused with the unrelated Stratton family of Chapter 14.

entities.name: John Melven
entities.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a grey fox skin in January 1742/3.

entities.name: Mr. Gilian Baker
entities.body: A Lincoln farmer near the pond whose household kept an unusual "winged cat," which Thoreau visited and describes in Chapter 12.

entities.name: Mr. Coleman
entities.body: Henry Coleman, the Massachusetts agricultural commissioner whose published farm reports Thoreau twice notes did not cover his bean-field.

entities.name: Luther Blanchard
entities.body: A Concord Minuteman wounded at the Battle of Concord, invoked as a point of comparison in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.

entities.name: Buttrick
entities.body: Major John Buttrick, who commanded the Concord Minutemen at the North Bridge; his order "Fire! for God's sake fire!" is echoed in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.

entities.name: Davis and Hosmer
entities.body: Isaac Davis and Abner Hosmer, the two Concord Minutemen killed at the Battle of Concord, named together as the human dead whose fate the ant battle's carnage is mock-heroically compared to.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The Greek epic poet; Thoreau keeps the Iliad on his table through the summer, reads a passage of it aloud in translation to a woodchopper acquaintance, and cites Alexander's habit of carrying it on campaign.

entities.name: Æschylus
entities.body: The Greek tragedian, named alongside Homer as a classic never yet printed in English translation worth the name.

entities.name: Virgil
entities.body: The Roman poet, named alongside Homer and Æschylus as a classic author.

entities.name: Alexander
entities.body: Alexander the Great, who is said to have carried the Iliad with him on his expeditions in a precious casket.

entities.name: Mîr Camar Uddîn Mast
entities.body: A poet Thoreau quotes on the pleasure of reading, comparing it to intoxication by wine.

entities.name: Damodara
entities.body: An epithet of Krishna in Hindu scripture; Thoreau quotes a saying attributed to him about the freedom of a vast horizon, spoken when his herds needed new pastures.

entities.name: king Tching-thang
entities.body: A legendary Chinese emperor (Tang of Shang); Thoreau cites the characters said to be engraved on his bathing tub, urging daily renewal.

entities.name: Confucius
entities.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted several times under different transliterations of his name (Confucius, Khoung-tseu, Con-fut-see) on knowledge, virtue, and neighborliness.

entities.name: Kieou-he-yu
entities.body: A great dignitary of the state of Wei, in the anecdote Thoreau quotes about sending a messenger to Confucius for news of his master.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher; Thoreau reproaches himself for having his Dialogues on the shelf and never reading them, and later discusses Plato's definition of man as "a biped without feathers."

entities.name: Zoroaster
entities.body: The ancient Persian religious teacher, invoked as an example of someone who had the same spiritual experience as a solitary hired man Thoreau knows, but treated it as universal wisdom rather than private singularity.

entities.name: Jesus Christ
entities.body: Named as one through whose liberalizing influence, along with all the worthies, a solitary man might commune and set aside sectarian religion.

entities.name: Abelard
entities.body: Peter Abelard, the medieval philosopher; Thoreau asks whether Concord could not hire some Abelard to lecture to it, as part of his argument that villages should fund culture as noblemen once did.

entities.name: Adam
entities.body: The first man of Genesis, cited as the origin of human tedium and ennui, and, with Eve, of the first clothing (the bower) worn before the Fall.

entities.name: Eve
entities.body: The first woman of Genesis, named with Adam as driven from Eden, and as first wearing the bower of Paradise before any other clothing.

entities.name: Adam Smith
entities.body: The Scottish economist, named alongside Ricardo and Say as the "political economy" a poor student is taught in college while graduating in debt.

entities.name: Ricardo
entities.body: David Ricardo, the British economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Say.

entities.name: Say
entities.body: Jean-Baptiste Say, the French economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Ricardo. His surname also happens to be an ordinary English verb, capitalized twice elsewhere at the start of a sentence; only this one mention names the economist.

entities.name: Sir Kenelm Digby
entities.body: The seventeenth-century English natural philosopher, quoted on the "vital spirits" attracted by fallow, exhausted soil.

entities.name: Kirby
entities.body: William Kirby, co-author with Spence of a standard entomology text, cited on insects' feeding habits and on the history of recorded ant battles.

entities.name: Spence
entities.body: William Spence, Kirby's co-author, cited alongside him.

entities.name: Thseng-tseu
entities.body: Zengzi, a disciple of Confucius, quoted on the soul's absence from itself when the appetite masters perception: "one eats, and one does not know the savor of food."

entities.name: Mencius
entities.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted on the thin margin that distinguishes men from brute beasts, and how easily the common herd loses it.

entities.name: Chaucer’s nun
entities.body: The Canterbury Tales narrator Thoreau quotes and attributes to "Chaucer's nun," on hunters not being unholy men. Chaucer's own name never appears in the text on its own -- only as part of this one phrase -- so there is no separate entry for Chaucer himself.

entities.name: Huber
entities.body: François Huber, the Swiss entomologist Kirby and Spence credit as the only modern author to have witnessed a battle of ants firsthand.

entities.name: Æneas Sylvius
entities.body: Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, quoted by Kirby and Spence for his circumstantial account of a battle of ants on a pear tree.

entities.name: Eugenius the Fourth
entities.body: Pope Eugene IV, in whose pontificate the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes is said to have taken place.

entities.name: Nicholas Pistoriensis
entities.body: An eminent lawyer said to have witnessed and related the history of the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes.

entities.name: Olaus Magnus
entities.body: The Swedish churchman and writer who records a second ant battle, quoted by Kirby and Spence.

entities.name: Christiern the Second
entities.body: Christian II of Denmark, the "tyrant" whose expulsion from Sweden the ant battle Olaus Magnus describes is said to have preceded.

entities.name: Polk
entities.body: James K. Polk, President of the United States when Thoreau's own witnessed ant battle took place, per his mock-scholarly dating of the event.

entities.name: Webster
entities.body: Daniel Webster, whose Fugitive-Slave Bill dates Thoreau's ant battle in Chapter 12, and who is later named, in Chapter 18, as the orator of an imagined national celebration presided over by God.

entities.name: Samuel Laing
entities.body: The travel writer quoted on Laplanders sleeping unclothed on snow in reindeer-skin bags.

entities.name: Winslow
entities.body: Edward Winslow, later governor of the Plymouth Colony, whose account of a diplomatic visit to Massasoit -- warmly received but poorly fed and lodged -- Thoreau quotes at length.

entities.name: Massasoit
entities.body: The Wampanoag sachem who received Winslow's Plymouth delegation, sharing what little food his people had.

entities.name: Benvenuto Cellini
entities.body: The Italian Renaissance artist and memoirist, whose account of a halo seen over his own shadow after a vision in prison Thoreau compares to a phenomenon he has observed himself.

entities.name: Guy Faux
entities.body: Guy Fawkes, the Gunpowder Plot conspirator, named in a quoted poem about the Baker Farm.

entities.name: William Gilpin
entities.body: The English writer on landscape aesthetics, quoted on the dimensions and origin of Scotland's Loch Fyne, used as a point of comparison for Walden's own depth.

entities.name: Michaux
entities.body: François André Michaux, the French botanist, quoted on the high price of firewood in early-nineteenth-century New York and Philadelphia.

entities.name: Nebuchadnezzar
entities.body: The Babylonian king; Thoreau notes, of his second-hand chimney bricks, that he did not find this name inscribed on them, unlike the ancient bricks of Babylon that supply Mesopotamian villages with building material.

entities.name: Franklin
entities.body: Sir John Franklin, the British Arctic explorer whose lost expedition was a major contemporary news story; Thoreau asks pointedly whether he is "the only man who is lost."

entities.name: Mr. Grinnell
entities.body: Henry Grinnell, the American philanthropist who funded search expeditions for Sir John Franklin.

entities.name: Mungo Park
entities.body: The Scottish explorer of West Africa, named among the explorers Thoreau urges his reader to become instead within their own mind.

entities.name: Lewis
entities.body: Meriwether Lewis, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named among the explorers of Chapter 18's closing exhortation.

entities.name: Clarke
entities.body: William Clark, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named alongside Lewis.

entities.name: Frobisher
entities.body: Sir Martin Frobisher, the English explorer who searched for the Northwest Passage, named among Chapter 18's explorers.

entities.name: Columbus
entities.body: Christopher Columbus, invoked as the model for exploring continents and worlds within oneself rather than geographic ones.

entities.name: Mirabeau
entities.body: The Comte de Mirabeau, quoted on having taken to highway robbery to test what resolution was needed to defy society's most sacred laws -- a resolve Thoreau calls manly but idle.

entities.name: Kabir
entities.body: The Indian poet-saint, whose verses are said to admit four different senses -- cited as a contrast to the demand, in Thoreau's own place and time, that writing admit only one interpretation.

entities.name: Crœsus
entities.body: The proverbially wealthy king of Lydia, invoked to argue that even his riches would not change what a person's true aims and means must be.

entities.name: Tom Hyde
entities.body: A tinker, hanged, whose last words on the gallows -- reminding tailors to knot their thread before the first stitch -- Thoreau offers as an example of truth over decorum.

entities.name: Champollion
entities.body: Jean-François Champollion, decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphics, invoked rhetorically to ask who will decipher the "hieroglyphic" of the sand foliage on the railroad bank.

entities.name: Calidas
entities.body: Kalidasa, the classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, whose play Sacontala Thoreau quotes for its image of golden pollen-dust.

entities.name: Jupiter
entities.body: The chief god of the Roman pantheon; commerce, Thoreau notes, does not clasp its hands and pray to him, and Hebe, cupbearer to Jupiter, is invoked as a symbol of perpetual youth and health.

entities.name: Ceres
entities.body: The Roman goddess of agriculture, to whom -- Thoreau argues -- modern farmers no longer sacrifice, worshipping the infernal Plutus instead.

entities.name: Plutus
entities.body: The Greek god of wealth, whom Thoreau says the modern farmer serves in place of Ceres.

entities.name: Saturn
entities.body: The Roman god of a legendary golden age, named as the ancestral king whose race the old Romans believed themselves alone left of, and again as the "prostrate Saturn of an older dynasty" one steps over on entering Thoreau's imagined communal hall.

entities.name: Minerva
entities.body: The Roman goddess of wisdom, invoked in an anecdote about her objection to a house Momus criticized for not being movable, and again as the master builder of an oil-and-wine-cellar-equipped villa.

entities.name: Aurora
entities.body: The Roman goddess of the dawn; Thoreau calls himself as sincere a worshipper of her as the Greeks, and all poets and heroes are called her children.

entities.name: Memnon
entities.body: The mythological son of Aurora, a byword for a statue that sang at dawn; invoked as the type of all poets and heroes, children of Aurora who emit their music at sunrise.

entities.name: Hygeia
entities.body: The Greek goddess of health, daughter of Æsculapius; Thoreau declines to worship her, preferring Hebe instead.

entities.name: Æsculapius
entities.body: The Greek and Roman god of medicine, named as Hygeia's father, "that old herb-doctor."

entities.name: Hebe
entities.body: The Roman goddess of youth, cupbearer to Jupiter and daughter of Juno; Thoreau prefers her worship to Hygeia's, calling her the power to restore gods and men to the vigor of youth.

entities.name: Juno
entities.body: The Roman queen of the gods, named as Hebe's mother.

entities.name: Atlas
entities.body: The Titan condemned to bear the world on his shoulders, invoked when Thoreau describes his own eagerness to improve the Hollowell farm.

entities.name: Hercules
entities.body: The Greek and Roman demigod hero; his twelve labors are compared, unfavorably, to the burdens Thoreau's Concord neighbors have undertaken, and his strength is invoked again when Thoreau feels "strength like Antæus" from his beans.

entities.name: Cerberus
entities.body: The three-headed dog guarding the underworld in Greek myth, invoked as a figure for any host's overbearing insistence on feeding a guest.

entities.name: Vulcan
entities.body: The Roman god of fire, to whom Thoreau says he sacrificed an old forest fence for firewood.

entities.name: Terminus
entities.body: The Roman god of boundaries, whom an old forest fence, past its usefulness, was said no longer to serve.

entities.name: Brahma
entities.body: The Hindu creator god, invoked in the parable of the artist of Kouroo, whose perfect staff becomes, at the moment of completion, one of the fairest of all of Brahma's creations.

entities.name: Vishnu
entities.body: The Hindu preserver god, named alongside Brahma and Indra as a deity the servant of a Brahmin priest is said to worship.

entities.name: Indra
entities.body: The Hindu king of the gods, named alongside Brahma and Vishnu, and invoked earlier as the detached spectator in the sky Thoreau imagines himself as, watching the stream of events from above.

entities.name: Thor
entities.body: The Norse god of thunder, whose hammer -- which only breaks things in pieces -- is contrasted with the gentler, more powerful persuasion of the spring thaw.

entities.name: Atropos
entities.body: One of the three Fates in Greek myth, who cuts the thread of life; Thoreau proposes her name for the unstoppable railroad engine, "a fate ... that never turns aside."

entities.name: Ulysses
entities.body: The hero of Homer's Odyssey, invoked as the model for sailing past the daily "whirlpool" of dinner "tied to the mast," resisting distraction.

entities.name: Achilles
entities.body: The hero of Homer's Iliad; Thoreau translates his rebuke to Patroclus aloud to a woodchopper acquaintance, and later imagines a red ant as "some Achilles" avenging a fallen companion in the battle of the ants.

entities.name: Patroclus
entities.body: Achilles' companion in the Iliad, whose sad countenance Achilles rebukes in the passage Thoreau translates aloud, and whom the avenging red ant of the battle scene is compared to avenging.

entities.name: Menœtius
entities.body: Patroclus's father, named in the Iliad passage Thoreau translates.

entities.name: Peleus
entities.body: Achilles' father, named in the same Iliad passage.

entities.name: Æacus
entities.body: Peleus's father and Achilles' grandfather, named in the same Iliad passage.

entities.name: the Myrmidons
entities.body: Achilles' warriors in the Iliad, named in the translated passage; Thoreau later calls the legions of battling ants in his wood-yard "these Myrmidons."

entities.name: Antæus
entities.body: The giant of Greek myth who drew his strength from contact with the earth; Thoreau says he got strength like his from cultivating his bean rows.

entities.name: the Sirens
entities.body: The mythological singers whose voices lured sailors to their deaths; Thoreau says he escapes the village's gossip by keeping his thoughts on high things, "like Orpheus," who drowned their voices with his own song.

entities.name: Orpheus
entities.body: The legendary musician of Greek myth, whose singing drowned out the Sirens' voices and kept him out of danger, a model Thoreau invokes for escaping the village's gossip.

entities.name: Robinhood
entities.body: The legendary English outlaw, named among those across history and rank who have all required a few sticks from the forest to warm them and cook their food.

entities.name: Goody Blake
entities.body: A character from Wordsworth's poem "Goody Blake and Harry Gill," named alongside Harry Gill in the same passage as Robinhood.

entities.name: Harry Gill
entities.body: The other title character of Wordsworth's poem, named alongside Goody Blake.

entities.name: Actæon
entities.body: The mythological hunter torn apart by his own hounds; Thoreau notes that the woods ring with hunting cries yet no fox bursts forth "pursuing their Actæon."

entities.name: Toscar
entities.body: A figure from the Ossianic poems, named as the father of the "beautiful daughter" mourned in a quoted verse.

entities.name: Pilpay
entities.body: The legendary Indian fabulist credited with the beast-fables of the Panchatantra, invoked (as "Pilpay & Co.") for having put animals to their best literary use as vehicles for human thought.

entities.name: Robin Goodfellow
entities.body: The mischievous sprite of English folklore (later Shakespeare's Puck), invoked as a figure for an erratic, meddling sun that helps by fits and starts rather than steadily.

entities.name: Reynard
entities.body: The fox of medieval beast-fable tradition, invoked generically for the fox a black chicken at Hugh Quoil's abandoned house is said to be "awaiting."

entities.name: Tell
entities.body: The legendary Swiss marksman; Thoreau says the punctuality the railroad has taught everyone makes them all "sons of Tell."

entities.name: Theseus
entities.body: The legendary Athenian hero, named alongside Hercules and Achilles in the quoted closing verses of Chapter 1 as an example of heroic virtue "for which antiquity hath left no name."

entities.name: Old Mortality
entities.body: The title character of Walter Scott's novel, an old man who wanders Scotland re-cutting the inscriptions on covenanters' gravestones; Thoreau compares his philosopher-visitor to him, "say rather an Immortality."

coverage: Entities: 1 central (Thoreau, the narrator, never named -- no bindable alias), no major, 10 supporting (the real local cast of Chapters 10-12 and 14, plus the Hermit/Poet dialogue tags), the rest reference. Five namesake/common-word collisions: Cato (Elder vs. Ingraham, location-scoped), Nutting and Stratton (each a Chapter 14 family vs. a Chapter 15 named individual, location-scoped), Adam (biblical vs. Adam Smith, resolved by longest-span-first with no scoping needed), and Say (the economist Jean-Baptiste Say vs. the ordinary verb "Say" capitalized at two sentence-openings, bound only by a location-scoped match, no global alias). No footnote-apparatus contamination between editions, unlike Aristotle's Politics.
